hero.alt: A school laboratory bench with a light microscope and onion skin slides

slides.title: Predict: look inside an onion skin
slides.subtitle: Sketch what you think ONE onion skin cell looks like under a microscope.

blocks.text: A wooden table with a whole red onion and a whole white onion beside a blue light microscope.
items: onions_and_microscope_table
A friendly flat cartoon of a wooden table holding one whole red onion and one whole white onion beside a blue light microscope, with a sunny window behind.

blocks.text: Which structures will you see in an onion skin cell? Will there be chloroplasts? Why?
In your practical book, sketch one onion skin cell. Label every structure you expect.
items: 1. List every structure you expect to see.
2. Will there be chloroplasts? Explain your reasoning.

do: Hold up a whole red or white onion so everyone can see it.
Students open their practical books. They work alone and in silence.
Start the 4-minute timer.
Walk around and glance at sketches. Do not correct anything.
say: This is the same onion our Nairobi student was slicing when the cut happened.
Today we will look inside ONE layer of its skin. We will not use our eyes. We will use a microscope.
Before we do that, sketch what you predict you will see. Label every structure you expect.
look_for: Scan at least 8 practical books while students write. Each has a sketch with at least 3 named structures.
Note anyone who cannot name a single structure.
if_then: If a student cannot name any structure, say: Think back to the plant cell diagram from Lesson 4. What did you see on it? Then seat them next to a peer who can name structures, and check them again in the Observe phase.
If a student asks 'Is this right?', say: Write what you think. We will test it soon.
notes.why_this_works: Writing a prediction before seeing anything makes students commit to an idea. Later, any difference between the prediction and the evidence creates real surprise. The common misconception is that every plant cell has chloroplasts. This slide brings that idea out into the open.
answer_key: Example sketch: a rectangular box with labels for cell wall, nucleus, cytoplasm and vacuole. Example prediction: 'Chloroplasts: yes, because the onion is a plant.' or 'Chloroplasts: no, because the onion grows under the soil.' Accept any prediction that has a reason. Do not correct it yet.

slides.title: Compare with your partner
slides.subtitle: Then join the next pair. Note where you agree and disagree.
slides.time_note: 2 minutes pair talk, then pairs join up

items: people :: What did you both include?
thinking :: What is different?
handshake :: Join the next pair. Note where you agree and disagree.

do: Pairs compare their predictions for 2 minutes.
Then each pair joins a neighbouring pair. They note agreements and disagreements in their books.
Walk around and listen for chloroplast predictions.
Choose the 4 pairs you will call on in the next slide.
say: Turn to your partner. Compare your predictions. What did you both include? What is different?
Now join the pair next to you. Write down where you agree and where you disagree.
notes.wait_time: Allow the full 2 minutes of pair talk before pairs join up
look_for: Pairs are comparing real structure names, not just saying 'same'.
Listen for at least one pair who predicted chloroplasts and one who did not.
if_then: If a pair says 'we have the same', say: Tell me one thing that is different, even a small thing, like a label or a shape.
If a pair has nothing to say, say: Tell your partner why you drew the structure you drew.
notes.why_this_works: Saying an idea aloud to a partner helps students check it before they share with the class. Students who are unsure feel safer speaking to one partner first.
answer_key: Example note: 'We both predicted a cell wall and a nucleus. We disagree about chloroplasts: we said yes, the other pair said no.'

slides.title: BEFORE — Our Predictions
slides.subtitle: Tell us ONE structure you predicted and WHY.

blocks.text: Tell us ONE structure you predicted. Why?
Every prediction goes on the board. Nobody is told they are wrong yet.
items: Hold your predictions.
In about 20 minutes, your microscope will tell us who was right.

do: Cold-call 4 pairs: one strong predictor, one who predicted chloroplasts, one who did not, and one who is unsure.
Write every predicted structure on the board under the heading BEFORE — Our Predictions.
Do not correct any error.
Ask: how many groups predicted chloroplasts? Write the count on the board. You will return to it in the Explain phase.
say: Tell me ONE structure you predicted and WHY.
Thank you. I am writing it on the board. I am not saying yes or no.
Hold your predictions. In about 20 minutes, your microscope will tell us who was right.
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds after the question, before choosing a pair
look_for: While you scan the books: every learner has a labelled sketch with at least 3 named structures.
Count of groups that predicted chloroplasts is written on the board.
Listen for the reason, not only the structure name.
if_then: If a pair gives a structure with no reason, say: Why did you expect to see that in an onion skin cell?
If a learner cannot name any structure, seat them next to a peer who can. Check their book again during the Observe phase.
If a pair says 'we were wrong', say: We have not looked yet. Hold your prediction until the microscope tells us.
notes.why_this_works: A public list of predictions makes the evidence trail visible to everyone. Not correcting yet keeps students curious. The common misconception that all plant cells contain chloroplasts can then be tested honestly.

slides.title: Demonstration: make an onion slide
slides.subtitle: Watch the teacher. Every step is said aloud.
slides.time_note: Teacher demonstration at the front bench

blocks.text: A school lab bench with a blue light microscope, glass slides, a dropper bottle, forceps and half an onion.
items: lab_bench_onion_slide
A friendly flat cartoon of a school laboratory bench holding a blue light microscope, three glass slides, a small dropper bottle, a pair of forceps and half an onion on a white tile.
onion :: Peel one thin, clear layer from the onion leaf.
hand :: Lay it flat on the slide with forceps. No folds.
droplet :: Add ONE drop of iodine stain onto the tissue.
book :: Lower the coverslip slowly at an angle. No air bubbles.

do: Stand at the front bench where all students can see.
Say each step aloud as you do it (think-aloud).
Show how to hold the coverslip with the mounted needle.
Remind students: no scalpels or razor blades. Onion layers are separated by hand and forceps only.
say: Step 1. I am peeling back one layer of the onion fleshy leaf. I use my fingernail to lift the thin, almost transparent inner epidermis.
Step 2. Using forceps, I lay the epidermis flat on the slide. No folds. Flat.
Step 3. I add ONE drop of iodine stain directly onto the tissue. Iodine stains starch and makes the nucleus visible.
Step 4. I lower the coverslip at an angle using a mounted needle. It is like closing a book slowly. This avoids air bubbles.
look_for: Every student can see the bench. Move students if they cannot.
Students are watching your hands, not talking.
if_then: If air bubbles get trapped, say: See the bubbles? I will lift it and lower it more slowly, like closing a book.
If glass breaks, say: Stop. Do not touch it. Tell me. Then put it in the designated sharps bin, not the general waste bin.
If a student has told you about an iodine allergy, say: You will use plain water instead of iodine today.
notes.why_this_works: A think-aloud lets students hear the reasons behind each step, not only see the steps. Fewer groups then make the same mistakes in their own practical.

slides.title: Demonstration: focus the microscope
slides.subtitle: Start at low power. Then look in silence for 10 seconds.
slides.time_note: 10 seconds of silent looking, then 3 responses

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph.

items: microscope :: Put the slide on the stage. Clip it.
magnifier :: Start at LOW power. Coarse focus first, then fine focus.

do: Place the slide on the stage and clip it.
Start at LOW power. Use the coarse focus wheel first, then the fine focus.
Ask for 10 seconds of silence while students look.
Then take 3 responses with hands up.
say: Step 5. I place the slide on the stage, clip it, and start at LOW power. I use the coarse focus wheel first, then fine focus.
What do you notice? I want 10 seconds of silence. Just look.
Now, hands up. What can you see?
notes.wait_time: 10 seconds of silence, then take hands
look_for: In the 3 responses, students describe what they SEE (shapes, edges, colours), not only names they remember.
if_then: If students only call out names, say: Tell me what you SEE first. Shapes, edges, colours.
If nothing is clear, say: I will refocus. Watch the coarse focus wheel.
notes.why_this_works: Silent looking slows students down. They notice more detail before they start talking and naming.

slides.title: Your turn: make and focus your slide
slides.subtitle: Groups of 3 or 4. Everyone follows the safety rules.
slides.time_note: Groups make slides and focus the microscope

items: goggles :: Wear goggles and a lab coat before you stain.
onion :: Peel one thin layer. Lay it flat with forceps.
droplet :: ONE drop of iodine. Lower the coverslip slowly.
microscope :: Low power first. Coarse focus, then fine focus.
eyes :: Take turns. Everyone must see the cells.

do: Groups of 3 or 4. Every student records in their own practical book.
Walk around the room every 3 minutes.
Ask the prompt questions at each group.
say: Is your coverslip flat?
Are you on low power first?
Can you see a cell wall? Trace it with your finger on the eyepiece.
look_for: At each group you visit: coverslip is flat, no large air bubbles, the group started on low power.
Every student in the group gets a turn at the microscope.
Safety rules are followed: goggles on, cables off the walkway, glass handled with care.
if_then: If a group cannot focus, demonstrate refocusing at their microscope.
If a group has folds or bubbles, say: Make a new slide. Lower the coverslip more slowly, like closing a book.
If a student has an iodine allergy, they use plain water instead of iodine.
If a group sees only some structures, say: Honest drawings are valid evidence. Draw what you see.
notes.why_this_works: Practising the technique straight after the demonstration helps students remember it. Circulating every 3 minutes catches problems early.

slides.title: Draw what you see
slides.subtitle: Draw ONLY what you see. Use your own practical book.
slides.time_note: Each student draws in their own book

blocks.text: Draw only what you can see.
items: Use a ruler for your label lines.

do: Write the five observation prompts on the board and leave them up: draw 3–4 cells at low power; draw 1 cell at high power; label; write 'I can / cannot see chloroplasts'; write the magnification for each drawing.
Each student draws at BOTH low and high power in their own book.
Walk around and read the books of at least 6 learners.
say: Draw 3 or 4 cells at low power. Then draw 1 cell at high power.
Draw only what you can see. Do not draw what you remember from a diagram.
look_for: In at least 6 books: two drawings (low and high power) and a magnification written below each.
Drawings show only what is seen. For example, the nucleus is drawn inside the cell wall, not outside.
Students are drawing, not copying from a textbook.
if_then: If a nucleus is drawn outside the cell wall, kneel to the learner's level and say: Look through the eyepiece again. Can you trace the outer boundary of the cell with your eye? That boundary IS the cell wall. Now draw only what you can see.
If a student draws a structure they cannot see, say: Can you see it in the eyepiece right now? If not, do not draw it.
If the magnification is missing, say: Write the magnification used under each drawing.
notes.why_this_works: Drawing makes students look closely and decide what matters. Writing the magnification builds an understanding of scale.
answer_key: Low power drawing: 3–4 rectangular cells fitted together, each with a clear outline (cell wall). Magnification written below, for example ×40.
High power drawing: 1 cell drawn large, showing the cell wall, vacuole, nucleus and cytoplasm. Magnification written below, for example ×400.

slides.title: Label your drawing
slides.subtitle: Five minutes left. Check your practical book now.
slides.time_note: Label, write, then two groups share

items: pencil :: Label: cell wall, cell membrane, vacuole, nucleus, cytoplasm.
eyes :: Write: 'I can / cannot see chloroplasts.'
ruler :: Write the magnification below each drawing.

blocks.text: Everyone needs at least ONE complete drawing with labels.

do: With 5 minutes left, say the line below and start the timer.
Walk around and check books.
Cold-call 2 groups to describe one structure they can see. Choose one group with a clear nucleus and one that saw a cell wall.
say: Everyone must now have at least ONE complete drawing with labels. Check your practical book now.
Group, tell me ONE structure you can see in your cells.
look_for: In each book you check: at least 4 labelled structures on each drawing.
Magnification is written below each drawing.
The chloroplast observation is written, in any words (for example 'I cannot see chloroplasts').
Do not tell students what the result should be.
if_then: If a book has fewer than 4 labels, say: Look again at your drawing. Which parts can you point to? Label those.
If a student writes the chloroplast sentence without looking, say: Look through the eyepiece one more time. Then write what you see.
If a group is not finished, say: Finish one complete drawing first. The second can be completed later.
notes.why_this_works: Labelling forces students to name what they actually see. The 5-minute check makes sure every student leaves with their own evidence for the Explain phase.
answer_key: Labelled drawing: ruler-drawn label lines to cell wall, vacuole, nucleus and cytoplasm (cell membrane only if the student can see it). Sentence: 'I cannot see chloroplasts.' Magnification written below each drawing, for example ×40 and ×400.

slides.title: Mark your predictions
slides.subtitle: Use a different colour pen. Open your prediction sketch.
slides.time_note: 2 minutes silent marking, then a hands-up count

items: check :: Circle every prediction your microscope confirmed.
cross :: Cross out every prediction that was wrong.

blocks.text: Hands up: Did you predict chloroplasts? Did you find them?

do: Point to the BEFORE — Our Predictions list on the board.
Students use a different colour pen or pencil. Silent work for 2 minutes.
Then count hands aloud: who predicted chloroplasts would be present? Who found them?
Compare with the count you wrote on the board in the Predict phase.
say: Open your practical book to your prediction sketch. Take a different colour pen or pencil.
Circle every prediction that your microscope confirmed. Cross out every prediction that was wrong.
How many people predicted chloroplasts would be present? Hands up. How many of you found them?
look_for: In at least 8 books you glance at, the marks are in a different colour.
Students mark their own predictions honestly, including crossing out wrong ones.
if_then: If a student does not want to cross out an idea, say: A wrong prediction is useful evidence. It shows us something new.
If a student marks everything correct, say: Look at your drawing from the microscope. Does it match each thing you predicted?
notes.why_this_works: Marking their own predictions in a new colour makes the change in thinking visible. The result is a clear before-and-after record.
answer_key: Example marked sketch: cell wall, nucleus and vacuole circled in a new colour. 'Chloroplasts present' crossed out, if it was predicted.

slides.title: Why are there no chloroplasts?
slides.subtitle: Think first. No hands up yet.
slides.time_note: 15 seconds of thinking, then 3 learners answer

blocks.text: Why are there no chloroplasts in onion skin cells?

items: thinking :: Think for 15 seconds. No hands up.

do: Say that the result is important.
Wait 15 seconds in silence.
Cold-call 3 learners. Choose one who predicted chloroplasts, one who did not, and one who has not spoken yet.
say: This is a significant scientific result. The question is WHY.
I want 15 seconds of thinking time. No hands yet.
Give me your best explanation for why there are no chloroplasts in onion skin cells.
notes.wait_time: 15 seconds of silence before any answer
look_for: In the 3 answers, listen for a reason (light, underground, the job of the cell) or only 'they don't need them'.
if_then: If a student says only 'they don't need them', say: Why don't they need them? Keep thinking. We will build the answer together on the next slide.
Do not give the full answer yet.
notes.why_this_works: Thinking time before speaking gives more students a real idea to share. The common misconception is that all plant cells contain chloroplasts. The students' own evidence has just challenged this idea.
answer_key: Example student answer: 'The onion bulb grows underground, so there is no light. The cell does not need chloroplasts.'

slides.title: Build the explanation together
slides.subtitle: Answer one question at a time.
slides.time_note: Click one question at a time

items: onion :: Where does the onion bulb grow?
sun :: Does light reach it?
leaf :: What do chloroplasts do?
question :: Would the cell build chloroplasts with no light?

blocks.text: Cell specialisation: each cell is built for its own job.

do: Click one question at a time. Take answers from different students.
Show the last line (cell specialisation) only after students have answered all four questions.
Then connect to the healing finger.
say: Let's build the full explanation together.
Where does the onion bulb grow? Does light reach it? What do chloroplasts do? So would it make sense for the cell to build chloroplasts if there is no light?
This is CELL SPECIALISATION. The onion epidermal cell is specialised for PROTECTION and STORAGE, not photosynthesis.
Just like the cells in our Nairobi student's finger are each specialised for one job: platelets for clotting, fibroblasts for collagen, epidermal cells for closing the wound.
look_for: Students answer with reasons: underground; no; photosynthesis, capturing light; no.
Cold-call students who did not speak in the last slide.
if_then: If a student says 'because it is white', say: Colour is a clue. What does the white colour tell us about light?
If students answer yes to the last question, say: What would a chloroplast need to work? Where does the onion bulb grow?
notes.why_this_works: A chain of small questions lets students build the idea from their own evidence. The idea gets its name only after they understand it.
answer_key: No, it would not make sense to build chloroplasts with no light.

slides.title: Write your explanation
slides.subtitle: Three sentences. Use your own words.
slides.time_note: Write alone in your practical book

blocks.text: In your practical book, write 3 sentences:
items: 1. What I observed.
2. Why this makes sense for the onion's function.
3. How this connects to the Nairobi student's healing finger.
droplet :: Platelets: clotting
link :: Fibroblasts: collagen
bandage :: Epidermal cells: close the wound

do: Students write alone in their practical books.
Walk around and read 4–5 responses as students write. Do not collect the books.
Leave the three healing cells on the screen as a reminder.
say: In your practical book, write 3 sentences: what you observed, why it makes sense, and how it connects to the healing finger.
notes.wait_time: The full writing time in silence
look_for: In 4–5 responses, each one mentions (a) the absence of chloroplasts, (b) the underground or no-light home of the onion bulb, and (c) a link to specialisation or the healing finger.
if_then: If a student writes only 'onion cells have no chloroplasts because they don't need them', prompt: Why don't they need them? What does a chloroplast DO? Where does the onion grow?
If a student writes no link to the finger, say: Look at the three cells on the screen. Each one has one job. How is the onion cell like them?
notes.why_this_works: Writing moves students from 'I saw X' to 'X tells us how cells work'. This is the most important thinking skill in the unit.
answer_key: Under the microscope I saw a cell wall, a nucleus, cytoplasm and a vacuole, but no chloroplasts. This makes sense because the onion bulb grows underground where light does not reach, so the cell does not need chloroplasts for photosynthesis. In the healing finger, platelets, fibroblasts and epidermal cells are each specialised for one job, and the onion cell is specialised too.

slides.title: Driving Question Board: write two notes
slides.subtitle: Why do cells look so different, and how does shape decide a cell's job?
slides.time_note: Each group writes two sticky notes

blocks.text: A classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes with small gold stars beside some of them.
items: dqb_sticky_notes_board
A friendly flat cartoon of a classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes, with three small gold stars stuck beside some notes, and a wooden desk with a pot of pencils in front.
Answer note :: One thing you can now say with evidence from YOUR microscope today.
Question note :: One new question your observation raised.

do: Give each group two sticky notes of different colours: one for ANSWERS and one for NEW QUESTIONS.
Groups write for 3 minutes.
Walk around and help groups that are stuck.
say: The Driving Question asks: Why do cells look so different, and how does shape determine the job a cell can do?
Today you looked at a real cell for the first time. On your ANSWER note, write one thing you can now say with evidence. Use your microscope today, not only the textbook.
On your QUESTION note, write one new question your observation raised. Something you still cannot explain.
look_for: Each answer note names something seen in today's practical, not only something recalled from a book.
if_then: If a group is stuck, say: What surprised you most today?
If a group has no question, say: What would you need to see next to understand the healing finger better?
If an answer note comes from the textbook, say: Can you re-write this using something you actually saw today?
notes.why_this_works: Splitting notes into 'evidence' and 'questions' shows students that science grows by gathering evidence and asking new questions together.
answer_key: Answer note: 'We can see cell walls in plant cells. Animal cells in the wound don't have these.'
Question note: 'Will animal cells have a cell wall?' or 'How does the fibroblast know to make collagen?'

slides.title: Post, read and vote
slides.subtitle: Does today's evidence support the answer?
slides.time_note: Post notes, read three aloud, vote

blocks.text: Post your notes under 'Evidence We Now Have' and 'Questions We Still Need to Answer'.

items: check :: Thumbs up: yes, well supported
thinking :: Thumbs sideways: partly
question :: Thumbs down: not sure yet

do: Groups post their notes on the Driving Question Board under the two headings.
Read 3 answer notes aloud. Choose notes that cite real observations.
For each note, ask for the thumbs vote.
Point at the board and talk about how it grows.
say: Does today's evidence support this answer? Thumbs up if yes, sideways if partly, down if we are not sure yet.
Look at our board. It is growing. Each lesson we add more.
By Lesson 12, we should be able to answer the driving question fully.
look_for: Every group posted at least one answer note that names a specific observation from today's practical.
Watch the votes. Note any answer where students are split.
if_then: If a note comes only from the textbook, hand it back and say: Can you re-write this using something you actually saw today?
If votes are split, say: What more evidence would we need?
If students vote thumbs up for everything, say: Which part of this answer did we actually see today?
notes.why_this_works: Voting on whether evidence supports a claim makes students judge the quality of evidence. This is a key habit of scientific reasoning.
answer_key: Example: 'We can see cell walls in plant cells. Animal cells in the wound don't have these.' Vote: sideways. We saw cell walls in onion cells today, but we have not yet looked at animal cells with our own microscope.

slides.title: Revise your model in a NEW colour
slides.subtitle: Your microscope gave you real evidence. Use it.

items: pencil :: Redraw or confirm the cell wall. Thicker or thinner than before?
plate :: Add the large central vacuole if it is missing.
leaf :: Chloroplasts: only in cells in light. Not onion skin. Not human cells.
memo :: Add a caption: 'This model is based on evidence from…'

do: Students open the unit model they have been building. They use a NEW colour.
Display the four revision prompts on the board.
Walk around. Check the chloroplast notes first.
Collect the practical books of one group (rotate groups each lesson) for written feedback. Return them before Lesson 7.
say: Open to your unit model. Today your microscope gave you real evidence.
Use a NEW colour to update your model.
Annotate chloroplasts carefully. Say where they are found and where they are not found.
look_for: In at least 8 models: one addition or correction in the new colour that comes from today's practical, not copied from a textbook.
The chloroplast note says where chloroplasts are present (cells exposed to light, for example leaf cells) and where they are not (onion epidermis, animal cells).
if_then: If a student copied a textbook diagram, say: Which part of your model comes from YOUR microscope today? Show me.
If the chloroplast note says 'plants have no chloroplasts', say: Which plant cells did you look at today? Where would chloroplasts be found?
If a student has no caption, say: Write the sources you have used so far in the unit.
notes.why_this_works: Using a new colour each lesson makes the growth of understanding easy to see. Giving the evidence source teaches students to say why they believe an idea. This also reduces the misconception that every plant cell has chloroplasts.
answer_key: Revised model: cell wall outline confirmed and drawn in a new colour. Large central vacuole added. Annotation: 'Chloroplasts: ONLY in cells exposed to light (for example leaf cells). NOT in onion epidermis, NOT in human cells.' Caption: 'This model is based on evidence from: the diagrams and discussion in Lessons 1–5 and our onion microscope practical in Lesson 6.'

slides.title: Predict: the next lesson
slides.subtitle: Write ONE sentence.
slides.time_note: Last 60 seconds of model time, then three read aloud

blocks.text: What will be DIFFERENT when we look at an animal cell next lesson?

items: thinking :: Think about platelets, neutrophils and fibroblasts from the Nairobi student's finger.

do: After 5 minutes of model work, say 'Last 60 seconds' and start the timer.
Students write one sentence in their books.
Cold-call 3 learners to read their prediction aloud. Choose students whose models showed a careful chloroplast note.
Point to the Driving Question Board to close.
say: Last 60 seconds. Write one sentence: what do you predict will be DIFFERENT when we look at an animal cell next lesson?
Hold that prediction. In Lesson 7 we test it.
We now have real evidence from a real cell. Our model is stronger. But we still have questions. That is exactly how science works.
look_for: Each sentence names at least one specific structural difference between plant and animal cells.
Check at least 8 books while students write.
if_then: If a sentence says only 'it will be different', say: Different how? Name one structure that plant cells have and animal cells may not.
If a student cannot start, say: Look at your chloroplast note in your model. What does it say about human cells?
notes.why_this_works: A one-sentence prediction links today's evidence to the next lesson. It gives students a reason to look carefully next time.
answer_key: I predict an animal cell will have no cell wall and no chloroplasts, because the onion cell showed that cells only have the structures their job needs.

build_log.sow_says: Unit data: 'Sub-Strand 1.3: Cell Structure and Specialisation'. Lesson: 'Sub-Strand 1.1: Cell Structure'. Meta: substrand_id 1.1.
build_log.deck_does: No sub-strand number is written on the phase slides.
build_log.why: The unit label (1.3) does not match the lesson and meta (1.1). The SoW owner should correct it.

build_log.slide: Revise your model in a NEW colour
build_log.sow_says: 'Learners return to the cumulative cell model they began in Lesson 1' (Lesson 6 Model Building). The storyline says Version 1 of the model is made in Lesson 2.
build_log.deck_does: Slides say 'your unit model' and do not say which lesson it started in.
build_log.why: The two statements disagree about when the model began. The SoW owner should choose one.

build_log.slide: Predict: look inside an onion skin
build_log.sow_says: 'the same onion our Form 1 student in Nairobi was slicing'
build_log.deck_does: Slides and notes say 'Nairobi student' (the SoW's own wording in the Explain and Model Building phases). The word 'Form 1' is not used.
build_log.why: 'Form 1' is not a CBE term. The manual says Grade 10, never Form. The SoW owner should update the phenomenon text.

build_log.sow_says: 'Iodine stains starch and makes the nucleus visible.'
build_log.deck_does: Keeps the sentence as a teacher say line.
build_log.why: Iodine reacts with starch. Onion epidermal cells store little starch, so the sentence may mislead. A teacher should check how the nucleus becomes visible with iodine.

build_log.sow_says: 'Label: cell wall, cell membrane, vacuole, nucleus, cytoplasm' and 'cell membrane pressed against the inner cell wall'
build_log.deck_does: Keeps cell membrane in the label list.
build_log.why: With a school light microscope the cell membrane is hard to see separately from the cell wall. Students may label it from memory instead of from evidence. Teacher checker to confirm.

build_log.sow_says: 'low power (×40) and high power (×100 or ×400)'
build_log.deck_does: Keeps these values in the table.
build_log.why: With a ×10 eyepiece, a 4× objective gives ×40, a 10× objective gives ×100 and a 40× objective gives ×400. ×100 is usually medium power, not high power. Magnification depends on the lenses of each school's microscope.

build_log.sow_says: 'After focusing, say: What do you notice? I want 10 seconds of silence — just look.'
build_log.deck_does: Shows the question and a 10-second timer. The notes do not say how the class sees the view.
build_log.why: The SoW does not say how the whole class sees the focused view (camera, projector or queue). Teacher checker to add a method that works in schools.

build_log.sow_says: The SoW gives times only for: silent sketch 4 min, pair talk 2 min, demonstration 10 min, group practical 25 min, marking 2 min, DQB notes 3 min, model revision 6 min (last 60 seconds for the prediction).
build_log.deck_does: Allocates the unstated parts so the phase slides total 74 minutes: Predict 12 (4, 4, 4), Observe 35 (6, 4, 9, 11, 5), Explain 12 (3, 2, 3, 4), Driving Question Board 8 (4, 4), Model Building 7 (5, 2). The remaining 6 minutes are unit map 1, goals 1, safety 2, summary 2.
build_log.why: The SoW has no times for sharing, class discussion, writing in Explain, posting, voting or cold-calls. The deck did not need to trim any activity. Teacher checker to confirm the times are realistic.

build_log.slide: Your turn: make and focus your slide
build_log.sow_says: The SoW names forceps, mounted needle, glass slide, coverslip, iodine stain, onion and compound light microscope, but gives no quantities or concentrations per group.
build_log.deck_does: Slides list no quantities. Part B glance slide must write only what exists.

build_log.slide: Your turn: make and focus your slide
build_log.sow_says: 'Microscope electrical cables must not trail across walkways', 'designated sharps bin', 'lab coats and safety goggles must be worn'
build_log.deck_does: Keeps all of these in notes without change.
build_log.why: Many schools use mirror microscopes and may not have a sharps bin, lab coats or goggles for every student. Teacher checker to check this against real school equipment.

build_log.sow_says: 'Hold your predictions. In about 20 minutes, your microscope will tell us who was right.'
build_log.deck_does: Keeps the sentence on the slide.
build_log.why: The Predict slides take 12 minutes and the demonstration takes 10 more, so students first use the microscope after about 22 minutes (plus the opening slides). 'About 20 minutes' is close but not exact.

build_log.sow_says: ARES resources are listed (plant and animal cell comparison videos, readings and practice).
build_log.deck_does: No ARES resource is placed on any phase slide.
build_log.why: The available titles compare plant and animal cells or show labelled plant cell structures. They would give away the chloroplast result or Lesson 7 before students record their own evidence. Part B decides the match notes on the glance slide.

build_log.sow_says: Lesson titles such as 'Microscopy Practical 1 — Observing Onion Epidermal Cells' and 'Consolidation, DQB Closure, and Final Explanation — The Healing Cut Fully Explained'.
build_log.deck_does: Unit map uses short titles of at most 6 words made only from words in each SoW title (for example 'Observing Onion Epidermal Cells', 'Human Cheek Cells', 'Final Explanation').
build_log.why: Shows every lesson without inventing names. The map titles for Lessons 6 and 7 drop 'Microscopy Practical 1/2'.

build_log.sow_says: Lesson purpose: 'identify key plant cell structures, and connect direct microscopic evidence to the anchoring phenomenon'; knowledge point (c): 'onion epidermal cells lack chloroplasts because onion bulbs are underground storage organs'.
build_log.deck_does: Goals and key words avoid naming the structures and avoid the chloroplast result. Goal 3 says 'Explain what your own evidence tells us about how cells are built for their jobs'.
build_log.why: Goals and key words are shown before Predict, so they must not give away the result.

build_log.sow_says: Five safety protocols, including 'lab coats and safety goggles must be worn during staining' and 'Learners with known iodine allergies... may use plain water as an alternative mountant'.
build_log.deck_does: Shows five short rules, one per SoW protocol, in plain language. Details such as the sharps bin are kept in the notes.
build_log.why: Five rules is the maximum. Teacher checker to confirm that goggles, lab coats, a sharps bin and plain water are available in real schools. Plain water will not stain the nucleus, so those students will see less.

build_log.sow_says: 'groups of 3–4'; forceps, mounted needle, iodine stain, glass slides, coverslips, onion, compound light microscope. No quantities or concentrations.
build_log.deck_does: Materials list names each item with 'one per group' only for the microscope, which fits the SoW's group practical. No iodine concentration or counts of slides, coverslips or onions.
build_log.why: The SoW gives no quantities. The teacher checker should add them for the class size.

build_log.sow_says: No fallback is given if microscopes or materials are missing.
build_log.deck_does: Fallback uses the manual's options: groups take turns, or the teacher focuses one microscope and students queue to look.
build_log.why: Needed by the manual (Section 9). Teacher checker to confirm it works in real schools.

build_log.sow_says: ARES resources: 'Comparing animal and plant cells', 'Plant vs animal cells', 'Overview of animal and plant cells', 'Plant Cell Structures (Flexbook)', 'Plant cell walls', 'Plant Cell Structures Practice'.
build_log.deck_does: Marks the first three as do_not_use and the last three as preview_first. No resource is placed on any slide.
build_log.why: The first three compare plant and animal cells and would spoil the chloroplast result and Lesson 7. The last three are about plant structures in general, not onion cells, and fit only after students have recorded their own drawings.

build_log.sow_says: 'gene expression is selective, and structure is determined by function'
build_log.deck_does: Keeps the SoW model answer unchanged in the notes.
build_log.why: Gene expression is not introduced in Lessons 1–5. The phrase may be beyond what Grade 10 students have met at this point. The SoW owner should decide whether to keep it.

build_log.sow_says: 'the onion epidermal cell is adapted for protection and storage, not photosynthesis'
build_log.deck_does: Keeps the sentence in the model answer.
build_log.why: The epidermis mainly protects the bulb. Storage is mostly done by the fleshy leaf cells beneath it. The wording may need checking by a teacher.

build_log.sow_says: Observed answer: 'cell membrane pressed against the inner cell wall'; Learned answer: 'a cell wall, vacuole, and nucleus' (membrane not listed).
build_log.deck_does: Keeps both answers as written.
build_log.why: The cell membrane is listed as observed in one place but not in the other, and it is hard to see with a school microscope. The SoW owner should make these consistent.

lesson_oneliner: Make your own onion skin slide and look at real cells under the microscope.
purpose: Students prepare a temporary wet mount of onion epidermis, stain it with iodine and observe it at low and high power.
Students gather their own first-hand evidence of plant cell structures and draw only what they see.
The class finds that the onion skin cells show no chloroplasts. This surprise leads into cell specialisation and the driving question.
The onion is the same vegetable the Nairobi student was slicing when the cut happened, so the anchoring phenomenon stays alive.
This is the move from models built from diagrams to models revised from evidence.
before_class: Test every microscope: light works, objectives click into place, coarse and fine focus turn.
Prepare onions, glass slides, coverslips, forceps, mounted needles and iodine with droppers. Quantities per group are not given in the SoW, so decide them for your class.
Check goggles and lab coats. Know where the sharps bin is. Keep microscope cables off walkways.
Ask before the lesson whether any student has an iodine allergy. Have plain water ready for them.
Write the headings BEFORE — Our Predictions, Evidence We Now Have and Questions We Still Need to Answer on the board or wall.
Write the five observation prompts and the four model revision prompts where they can be shown later.
Prepare two colours of sticky notes for each group.
Check students have their practical books, their unit model and a different colour pen.
Decide how the class will see the focused view during the demonstration (camera, projector or queue to look).
do_not_show: Do not show the slides 'Why are there no chloroplasts?' and 'Build the explanation together' until students have recorded their own drawings and marked their predictions.
Do not show any ARES video or reading about plant or animal cells before students have drawn their own onion cells.
Do not show the Summary Table slide until the Model Building slides are finished. Keep the answer key in the notes only.
Do not tell students what they should see in the microscope before they have recorded it.
so_far: You have built a cell model and studied plant and animal cell diagrams.
goals: Prepare a temporary slide of onion skin and observe it with a light microscope.
Describe the structures you see, using a labelled drawing with magnification.
Explain what your own evidence tells us about how cells are built for their jobs.

key_words.definition: A thin piece of tissue in a drop of liquid under a coverslip, made for a short look.
A coloured liquid that makes parts of a cell easier to see.
How many times bigger the image looks than the real thing.
A clear pencil drawing of only what you see, with labels and magnification.
When a cell is built for one particular job.

safety.title: Safety first
rules: Iodine can irritate. Keep it off skin and eyes. Wear goggles and a lab coat when you stain.
Glass breaks easily. If it breaks, stop and tell the teacher. Never put it in the general waste bin.
No scalpels or razor blades. Separate onion layers with your hands and forceps only.
Keep microscope cables off the walkway.
Allergic to iodine? Tell the teacher before we start. You will use plain water.

do: Read each of the five rules aloud and point to the matching equipment.
Ask: has anyone told me about an iodine allergy? Check that names match your list.
Check that goggles and lab coats are available before staining starts.
Show where the sharps bin is.
During the practical, watch for iodine on hands, loose glass and cables across the walkway.
say: Safety first. We use iodine today and it can irritate your skin and eyes.
Goggles and lab coats on before you stain.
Glass slides and coverslips break easily. If one breaks, stop, do not touch it, and call me.
We do not use scalpels or razor blades today. Hands and forceps only.
If you have an iodine allergy, tell me now. You will use plain water.
notes.why_this_works: Rules that match today's real hazards are easier to remember than a long list. Saying them before students touch anything prevents most accidents.

glance.fallback: If microscopes are short, groups take turns while others prepare slides. Or the teacher focuses one microscope and students queue to look. Students still draw only what they see.

resource_notes.note: Shows plant and animal cell differences, including chloroplasts, which would give away the Predict answer. Use after 'Build the explanation together', or in Lesson 7.
Plant vs animal practice would pre-empt the chloroplast prediction. Use as revision after 'Write your explanation', or in Lesson 7 with the cheek cells.
A general overview that shows the structures students should find themselves. Use after 'Revise your model in a NEW colour', or as revision.
Useful labelling reference for plant structures. Check its diagrams do not push chloroplasts before students draw. Best kept for 'Label your drawing' or the model revision.
Cell walls are visible in onion cells, but the video probably does not explain missing chloroplasts. Check it before using it after 'Why are there no chloroplasts?'
Practice questions on plant cell structures. Check they match the onion cell structures students saw. Use after 'Write your explanation' as consolidation.

summary.observe_prompt: Describe your onion cell drawings: the shape of the cells, the parts you saw and any part you did not see.
summary.learn_prompt: Which structures do onion skin cells have, and which one is missing? Why?
summary.explain_prompt: Link the onion cell to the cells that healed the Nairobi student's finger.
summary.next_lesson: We look at cells from your own body to test your prediction.
summary.answer_observe: Onion epidermal cells prepared as temporary wet mount slides stained with iodine: rectangular cells with a visible cell wall, a large central vacuole, a nucleus stained dark brown or yellow by iodine, cytoplasm, and a cell membrane pressed against the inner cell wall. No chloroplasts observed.
summary.answer_learn: Onion epidermal cells are plant cells that have a cell wall, a vacuole and a nucleus, but no chloroplasts, because the onion bulb grows underground and is not exposed to light. This is evidence of cell specialisation: the onion epidermal cell is adapted for protection and storage, not photosynthesis. All plant cells share some features (cell wall, vacuole) but differ in which organelles they contain, depending on their function.
summary.answer_explain: The absence of chloroplasts in onion skin cells is not an error. It is evidence of specialisation. Cells only build and maintain the structures they need for their specific job. Just as the cells healing the Nairobi student's cut finger are each specialised (platelets for clotting, fibroblasts for collagen, epidermal cells for surface repair), the onion epidermal cell is specialised for its role. This confirms that having the same DNA does not mean every cell builds the same structures. Gene expression is selective, and structure is determined by function.
reflection: EVIDENCE QUALITY: Did every student draw a labelled drawing with at least 4 structures at both low and high power? If not, was it a focusing skill, a labelling vocabulary or a time problem? Adjust Lesson 7 timing.
THE CHLOROPLAST MOMENT: Did the absence of chloroplasts cause real surprise and good discussion? If students already knew it, open Lesson 7 with a more provocative prediction.
CER WRITING: How many students linked their observation to the healing finger? If fewer than 60%, begin Lesson 7 with a 3-minute re-read of the phenomenon.
DRIVING QUESTION BOARD: Are the new questions specific and forward-pointing, or vague? If vague, give the routine more support.
SAFETY: Were all safety rules followed without prompting? Note any group that needed reminders about goggles or broken glass and address it at the start of Lesson 7.
